How can this be spoken of in the same breath as The Incredibles and Coraline? Its "forecast" is accurate in the same way a fortune cookie might: "misfortune will come soon." Broad and cynical, the exact type that people can easily see if they squint. I did not feel anything for the romance between these two bots and found Wall-E not particularly compelling. Wall-E (the film) is like one of the titular robot's garbage cubes: a thoughtlessly compressed collection of artifacts from a past world its creators don't understand. The "homages" to space odyssey 2001, 50s musicals, and early video gaming are just as arbitrary as any collection of silverware and trash lids to come out of the compactor. Simply alluding to a glorious past where "things existed" doesn't suffice. What should these pleasureslaves be doing instead? Watching Pixar films on Disney+? Why is this better than drinking sodas and looking at your floating iPad? There is an answer to this, but Wall-E doesn't have it. If you just want to amuse your children then it will get the job done, at least after that dull first act.

I had to watch WALL-E twice. The first time, it barely left any impression, and I was surprised to find that the ample enjoyment I received from Ratatouille, Inside Out and Finding Nemo, and the easy praise I was subsequently able to give them, were not forthcoming here. It wasn’t easy to say exactly why, though it certainly seemed apparent that its plot didn’t tick along with the buoyancy with which those three movies’ narratives had fizzled. So I came back a few weeks later and I watched it again. My reaction was roughly the same, though I felt I was perhaps able to identify the film’s intentions a little better- basically, I think its titular character, a small robot, is meant to evoke bittersweet notions of incredibly touching, Chaplin-esque naivety, as is his ‘relationship’ with EVE, a sophisticated lady robot, which eschews traditional dialogue and is expressed almost completely through action and inflection. It’s an understated film, then, and I guess such understatement is to be commended. It’s also something of a risk, and unfortunately it was a risk that didn’t really pay off for me. I can imagine very young children finding it enchanting, as they themselves communicate without full speech, but the adventures of WALL-E, who is clearly shown to be possessing great traits of pluck, determination and heart, left me with a set of dissatisfied queries, not least the Socratic question of whether one can really be considered ‘brave’ when they are not cognisant enough to recognise danger or even know that it exists. Elsewhere, live-action footage of Fred Willard is interspersed with the animation. Why? Why didn’t they get him to do a voice role and animate his character too, thereby making the movie visually consistent? Such a gripe may come across trivial and petty, and it is, but it’s also an incongruity which helps to indicate, albeit indirectly, why I wasn’t particularly convinced or compelled by WALL-E. Far be it for me to say that this movie isn’t ‘good enough’ or that it should have been executed differently. Like all Pixar movies, it looks fantastic, with a sequence that sees WALL-E and EVE perform, with fire extinguishers, an iridescent double-helix ‘dance’ out in the void of space being a particular highlight. But overall, it just didn’t really click for me. It was okay- that’s all, just okay, and in the context of the other three Pixar films I’ve covered, that signifies a significant depreciation. Positive Aspects: Considering that WALL-E’s intended audience is children, I think the film’s visual imagery of a trash-covered Earth serves as an effective introduction to society’s pollution problem. The endless mountains of compacted trash shown in the opening scenes are daunting to see. However, these images are not entirely exaggerated, as waste accumulation is an ongoing environmental issue in the real world. In fact, the global waste crisis is driven not simply by individual disposal habits, but also by reliance on consumption under capitalism and other systematic factors (Heiges & O’Neill, 2022). This connects to the film’s portrayal of a society that prioritizes constant consumption without considering the environmental consequences. BNL’s advertisements and widespread presence throughout the film further emphasize how corporations encourage people to continuously purchase and consume products. Through visual storytelling, particularly the widespread presence of BNL logos, the film introduces the relationship between consumer behavior and environmental degradation in a way that is easy for children to understand. Instead of relying entirely on dialogue to explain the consequences of pollution, Andrew Stanton uses the absence of humans on Earth, abandoned buildings, mountains of trash, and deserted landscape to communicate the severity of the problem. Through its visual depiction of a decayed Earth, WALL-E encourages younger audiences to critically examine the consequences of excessive consumption and the importance of addressing waste. Additionally, the film’s visual storytelling encourages viewers to reflect more about their own consumption habits and long-term environmental consequences of a society built around convenience and continuous purchasing. By presenting these consequences through imagery than dialogue, the film’s message is more accessible to younger audiences while encouraging them to consider how their actions today may affect the environment in the future. Interesting Aspects: One interesting aspect is that WALL-E and EVE’s names and story serve as a direct nod to the biblical story of Adam and Eve. Adam and Eve are biblical figures most famously known for disobeying God by eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. A notable part of their story is that God created Eve as his companion. Similarly, WALL-E is a lonely robot living on a trash-covered Earth, while EVE is sent by BNL to search for vegetation. Although their initial purposes are different, EVE eventually becomes WALL-E’s companion, and the two develop a close relationship. I find Stanton’s choice to retell elements of the biblical story through two robots rather than humans particularly interesting. The parallels are especially thought-provoking because the film takes a story traditionally associated with the creation of humanity and reimagines it through artificial beings. I believe this decision offers a satirical critique of humanity. While humans have abandoned Earth because of the environmental destruction caused by their own consumption, two robots become the catalysts for humanity’s eventual return and the planet’s restoration. In this sense, Stanton reverses the traditional creation narrative by presenting artificial beings as the ones who help establish the possibility of a new beginning for humanity. The biblical symbolism is ironic because the very beings created by humans ultimately help repair the damage that humanity caused. Negative Aspects: While WALL-E and EVE are robots, I find Stanton’s decision to assign them gendered characteristics and place them in an implied hetrosexual romantic relationship questionable. As human-made objects, the robots do not have biological sex in the same way humans do. Instead, their gender is communicated primarily through their character designs and behaviors. WALL-E is characterized by rusty, boxy shapes and a mechanical appearance, features typically associated with masculinity. In contrast, EVE is characterized by smooth, rounded shapes and sleek white armor, which gives her a more traditionally feminine appearance. Although these design choices are not inherently problematic, they become more questionable when the film establishes a romantic relationship between the two robots. WALL-E’s romantic interest in EVE stems from his imitation of the romantic gestures and behaviors displayed by the male suitors in the musical he watches. Rather than developing his understanding relationships independently, WALL-E models his romantic behavior after the conventional courtship portrayed in human entertainment. This reinforces heteronormality by presenting a conventional male-female romantic dynamic as the model for romantic relationships, even between artificial beings that do not have biological functions. Furthermore, I think the film misses an opportunity to explore a meaningful relationship between robots that does not necessarily have to develop into romance. Their companionship could have demonstrated the importance of platonic friendship without relying on romantic attraction.

Why do children not deserve stuff like this anymore? If you have watched media produced for kids in the last decade or so then you have probably felt an intuitive difference, but what is that exactly? In 1997 when the Teletubbies premiered in the UK, a small, vocal group of parents complained that the baby talk on the show was stunting the growth of their children’s speech. They found them imitating the eponymous creatures’ babbling and upper-middle-classedly wrote panicked letters to the Radio Times. So, is this what it’s all about? Are shows for kids worse now because we are overprotective and anything interesting gets cut to appeal to the highest-coddling-progenitor? Probably partially. Since 2010 it’s become more common to give “child development consultants” more direct control over the story and content of the shows they work on. This is downstream of demand from parents for more socially and morally enriching TV for their spawn. Basically an extension of libbed out wokeness gone mad, right? Not really. The idea of how many calories or how much protein was in the food you were eating would be a foreign concept to even the discerning eaters of the 19th century. This has changed into something we care very much about through advances in biological understanding, as well as the amount of control we have over what we eat. When you understand something, and feel like you have a choice, we feel we must exercise that choice. We now feel that we understand what makes us, and by extension our children, happy in life, and which interventions we can make in order to be good people. Any psychologist will tell you these interventions are most effective on a young and plastic brain. If you asked someone born in 1850 whether they thought it was important for their child to eat a high-fibre diet, it wouldn’t be so much that they “didn’t care” and more that they’d never thought about it, or didn’t feel like they knew what that meant exactly. This is much closer to the attitude of an average 70s parent towards the content of their children’s television show. Paw Patrol is the Huel of kids TV. Consciously refined and scientifically optimised and bland and disgusting. As more consumers demand products that meet a new need they now know they have, they are often exploited by producers who know that said consumers don’t fully understand what it is that they want. Check your “high protein” bread - this incomplete wheat protein doesn’t meet any of the needs of the average consumer that wants to eat high amounts of protein. The optimisation starts to become bad faith. If you really spend time looking at the packaging and advertising for Doritos or Coke or any similar mass market food product, you will start to feel creeped out in the same way you do watching whatever brain-melting slop you nephew has on his iPad. Look at that woman on the packet smiling, no one loves Doritos THAT much. You can’t help but think about who actually designed the product. Who signed off on it? They must be at least somewhat cynical to the whole thing right? It conjures the image of an exec smugly rubber-stamping our slop and we think “I bet he doesn’t even eat Doritos/I bet she doesn’t even let her kids watch Cocomelon.” And they probably don’t. Of course, shows like Cocomelon that ruthlessly optimise for a child’s attention are a slightly different phenomenon. Reported they run tests by putting a child in front of their programme with a second “Distractatron” screen to measure how effectively they can hack the poor bugger’s brain into complete fixation. Horrific as this is, at least parents know what they’re doing here. They’re not fooled into thinking some kind of moral lesson is being imbibed, that it’s nourishing. It’s Dominos for dinner, it’s buying your 5 year old COD: Black Ops. Something that we have historically relied on is that the person most exposed to a product is the same person making it. The local baker probably won’t put too much salt in his bread because he tries it more often than anyone. Films like WALL-E feel like the last generation of kids entertainment where the people making it subjected themselves to their own work in an unironic and serious way. To reuse the earlier analogy: they didn’t cynically add high fructose corn syrup and protein powder for the masses and then go home and eat whole foods from the farmers market. I agree with the psychologist that a child’s brain is plastic and sensitive, however I think this makes it all the more important that they are not exposed to what passes for children’s entertainment these days. What I see on their tablets is contrived, saccharine and totalitarian. It can prepare them for nothing and constructs a simplistic and fragile moral shell which will, ironically, stunt them socially. Kids are ravenous for real stories, uncomfortable and shocking and untidy. WALL-E didn’t really happen (I think?) but it at least attempts what all worthwhile fiction should, to say something true.

Y creo que probablemente no la había vuelto a ver después de que dejé de ver Disney Channel en televisión, es decir, al menos unos 15 años. Y nada, de verdad que curioso como puede pasar tanto tiempo y recordar una parte tan formativa de lo que lo hizo a uno ser como es. Que por cierto, estoy seguro que está mierda me radicalizó de niño JAJAJAJ. No sé, cuando era chiquito WALL-E lo era todo para mí, quizás porque también me sentía completamente Awkward todo el tiempo. Pero la verdadera sorpresa es verme tanto en él a estas alturas de mi vida. Y que 15 años después siga entendiendo por completo y teniendo esa conexión con un personaje me parece una cosa muy brutal. Es que no se cómo explicarlo pero somos la misma persona :p solo que él es heterosexual supongo aunque los robots no tienen género pero anyway ustedes me entienden (igual es medio cacorro porque su diva pop es Bárbara Streisand lol). Y no sé, igual que el caso de Mini Espías que los vi hace unos días, creo que son de esas películas que nos recuerdan que el cambio siempre puede estar en los más pequeños, los más awkward, los más raros. Ni qué decirles de la escena en qué los robots cascados organizan la revolución al son de la música.  (Que entre otras cosas hay tantos detalles pequeños, como ese, que nunca había cogido de esta película y que son la cosa más puramente maravillosa que haya visto en la vida) No sé, de verdad tuve una experiencia trascendental y de autoconocimiento muy grande volviendo a ver esta película jajaja. Y, en estos tiempos de mucha depresión, me ayudó a recordar muchas de las cosas que me hacen feliz y por las que me levanto cada día. Sea para recolectar trinkets históricos de los que no one cares about y luego mostrárselos a mis personas cercanas o para evitar que las megacoporaciones monopólicas nos quiten lo último de humanidad que tenemos, hoy WALL-E me recordó que siempre hay una razón para laventarse todos los días. En fin, el tiempo es una construcción social, porque no se si fue por el vino picho que saque de la tienda de mi mamá o por el grave estado de mierdero mental en el que me encuentro, pero me siento como si hubiera retrocedido en el tiempo. Me sentí en la sala de cine cuando fuimos a verla por la primera vez, me sentí en mi casa frente a mi mini televisor comiendo sándwich de atún y viéndola a las 7 PM, me sentí en casa :). Y ya, WALL-E la mejor película del mundo, se ganó su puesto en mi top 4. Me verán el siguiente Halloween disfrazado de WALL-E como quise toda la puta vida desde que vi esta película y nunca lo pude hacer. :p. Dos likes y disfrazo a Aureliano de cucaracha porque tenemos exactamente la misma relación que WALL-E y Hal. Por cierto, muerte a las megacoporaciones, muerte a los monopolios, muerte a quienes no protejan las leyes ambientales, y muerte a los Estados Unidos porque I'm sure que tuvieron todo que ver con este problema. Wall•e conhece Eva e acompanha alguém que afeta diretamente na "vida" do robô, a sua ingenuidade, seu conhecimento limitado e sua solidão são surpreendidas por Eva, Eva faz coisas que Wall•e jamais viu, Capacidade destrutiva, velocidade para montar um cubo mágico e suas risadas. Wall•e amou Eva e seu objetivo se tornou tocar as mãos de quem ele desenvolveu sentimentos. E ao fim, ambos terminam juntos, em um toque de mãos, em um choque que faz com que um robô recuperei suas memórias e um abraço. Wall•e é uma obra de arte por vários motivos, e provavelmente é repertório de bolso em temas ambientais, mas com toda certeza, ao meu ver se destaca pela arte do descobrir.

The opening was beautiful, Wall-E just loving all his little findings, finding joy in the little things, anything that piques his interest he loves and he is JUST himself. Something not many can do nowadays especially is just be them and love who they are and embrace it. Then there’s his relationship with Eve, it’s simply beautiful. He knows what he wants and he fights for it and for her without skipping a beat, again, knowing what he loves and refusing to do anything but be who he is. I didn’t think a movie about robots would get me to shed tears but there I was wiping my tears away to end the movie. Amazing animation, amazing story, amazing execution, and amazing credit animation to give you an idea of what that future was and became. Bravo…. Just fucking bravo.
